en: *Vajraśekhara-sūtra-prathama-yoga-samantabhadra-bodhisattva-japa-vidhi*,
one fascicle.
Appointed to the rank of Kaifu Yitongsi, Teci, and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
I take refuge and pay homage to Samantabhadra, the essence of the *dharmadhātu* and *tathatā*.
Now, relying upon the Great Teaching, I shall briefly describe the ritual for practice of the Supreme Vajraśekhara. The Supreme Vajraśekhara.
The assembly of noble ones gathered like the ocean, Granting compassion and bestowing protection, Benefiting those who practice; Therefore, this has been compiled.
If one desires to seek liberation, One must rely upon the ācārya.
Seek to receive the empowerment; once permission has been granted, one should then practice according to the fundamental teachings.
Having selected an excellent location, establish the maṇḍala-cakra, and one should immediately visualize oneself [as the deity].
Identical in essence to that Samantabhadra, White in color like a conch or snow,
seated upright in samādhi, Visualize upon his tongue a pure and wondrous five-pronged vajra; Recite this mantra in secret.
The same pure dharmadhātu—recite the mantra as follows:
By reciting this mantra, the vessel of the body becomes completely purified;
then visualize the Buddhas filling the void like sesame seeds.
Then, reciting the *Samantabhadra-buddhanusmṛti-sūtra*, one clearly beholds all the Buddhas;
fulfilling the conduct of Samantabhadra, one seeks to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment with body and mind unshakable,
prostrating to all Buddhas within meditative concentration.
Having formed the great mudrā of the *iṣṭadevatā*, next bind the vajra-palms by joining them upright and interlacing the tips of the fingers.
Reciting the mantra as follows constitutes the vajra-bond; the vidyā is set forth below.
To open the bonds and strike the heart, one should recite the mantra as follows:

First, perform the *vajrabandha* (vajra-binding); then, with the thumbs and ring fingers opened, recite the *samāveśa-mantra* (mantra of universal entry). May [the deity] descend and grant protection at every moment.
Without altering the preceding mudrā, add the powers of dhyāna and prajñā;
this is called the *samādhi-muṣṭi*. Recite the mantra in this manner, then divide that fist into two:
the left in *māna* (pride) and the right at the heart.
The Vajra Body, Speech, and Mind: the physical form follows the initial visualization;
using the previous binding as the standard, with Wisdom and Power at the gates, one presses into the center—this is the Secret Samaya-mudrā.
At the heart, forehead, throat, and crown, one recites this mantra.
Furthermore, performing the vajra-bind, form the shape of a sword with the *kṣānti* (ring) and *praṇidhi* (little finger);
press the *tarjanī* (index) and *madhyamā* (middle) fingers against the side of the blade, according to the first [mudrā] of the first section.
Pressing the dhyāna-mudrā at the tip of wisdom,
as if in the posture of the full lotus (*paryaṅka*), one should visualize the Buddha Vairocana,
solemn and brilliantly white, shining radiantly; then recite this mantra:
Next, one should seal the forehead; one should visualize Akṣobhya, blue in color, situated in front.
After reciting these mantra syllables, one should then place [the hand] upon the right side of the crown of the head; his name is Ratnasaṃbhava.
Yellow in color and of majestic appearance, recite the mantra in this manner and place it upon the crown of the head.
The Tathāgata Amitāyus is red in color and of extraordinary form; recite this mantra, saying:
Furthermore, at the crown of the head on the left is the green Amoghasiddhi, surrounded by the five Buddhas.
Reciting these mantra syllables, one next forms the jewel-garland mudrā; through this empowerment, the body is adorned.
Using the two vajra-fists, one then winds them around in front of the forehead;
again separating the fists, they are placed behind the head as before.
Then, binding the garland, one slowly opens the hands from the *tana* and *prajñā* fingers, letting them fall down on both sides like wings.
If one visualizes hanging silk ribbons, recite the subsequent mantra;
with both the wings of concentration and wisdom fully extended, the mudrā of clapping is accomplished, which can please all the holy ones. Recite the mantra in this manner.
The mantra and mudrā of Vajramāna: silently recite it once in the heart, and again as above.
Adorned with the crown of Vajrasattva, whose body has the colors of the five Buddhas, one abides in the corresponding mudrā.
The Bhagavān Samantaprabha abides in the mudrā of the Tathāgata-fist;
next, one performs the Akṣobhya-mudrā: forming a fist with the fingers of the samādhi hand holding the corner of the robe, one places it upon the heart;
the wisdom hand touches the earth according to the ritual.
Ratnasambhava holds the wish-granting jewel; Amitābha’s supreme mudrā has the wisdom hand raised toward the breast;
The samādhi fist of Acala haughtily grasps a lotus, while the wisdom fist resembles a blooming flower—just like the Buddha Akṣobhya.
The mudrā of Amoghasiddhi has three banners on the crown of the head;
like one rescuing sentient beings, the palms are raised beside the breasts.
Furthermore, for the Vajrabandha, join the palms with the thumbs and wisdom fingers (jñāna-aṅguli) joined.
The *dāna* and *prajñā* [mudrās] are straight like mountain peaks;
the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* [mudrās] enter into the palms, joined together in the shape of an arrow.
One should apply these to the heart, forehead, throat, and crown of the head, all while employing the secret mantras of the mind.
Then, holding up the fragrant water and reciting the subsequent *argha* mantra, offer it near the forehead according to the ritual. Bathe the assembly of holy ones as prescribed;
as before, visualize the full moon, its brilliant white radiance appearing within the mandala.
The Great Sage abides within this space, dwelling in union with Vajragarva;
furthermore, the positions of the four deities are set forth:
the Eye-Arrow is before him, red in color and clad in robes, adorned with a crown and a garland.
With two hands bent in the gesture of drawing a bow and arrow,
he gazes upon the Sattva Kīlikīla; his color is white,
and he stands to the right with two hands in the vajra-fist, embracing the samaya in union.
In the rear is Rāga (Passion), whose name is so designated; his form and attire are entirely blue.
With both fists raised at the wisdom arm, he supports the elbow with the samādhi-feather and together they grasp the Makara banner; on the left is named Māna (Pride).
The body is yellow, with fists at the hips; slightly bowing the head to the left, perform the *karmamudrā* and recite the mantra.
Having empowered and firmly established the Great Holy Vajragarva, one should recite the heart-mantra.
Next, the various deities are further presented:
beginning with the Eye-Arrow, both fists are firmly clenched;
having completed the secret mudrā of the gesture of drawing the bow and releasing the arrow, recite the secret mantra as follows.
As before, form the two fists with both hands; cross the arms and clasp them against the chest.
While reciting the following phrase, change the previous mudrā:
extend the wisdom arm straight like a banner.
The mudrā of concentration rests between the elbows; recite the vidyā. This is called the Mudrā of Love.
The two fists each rest upon the hips, and by tilting the head to the left, the characteristics of the Mudrā of Slowness are thus accomplished. Recite the mantra as follows:
Next, the inner offerings are set forth: first, in the southeast corner, one holds a flower;
the form and attire are white. Vajra-sukha (Vajra Delight) and Vajra-sukha-svabhāva (Vajra Nature of Delight) are black in color and hold incense burners.
Offer a lamp to Vajranetra; his color is red, adorned with ornaments, and *urumaka* is used as the unguent.
Vajramahāśrī is yellow in form and substance; next, arrange their respective mudrās.
First, perform the dance with both fists;
then, according to the ritual, form the two vajra-fists side by side, cast them upward and scatter them, visualizing them as offering exquisite flowers. Recite the mantra as follows:
Clasping the fists, one then casts them downward; reciting "The clouds and seas of incense pervade all things," one performs the two-fisted mudrā with the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* fingers joined,
as prescribed in the subsequent mantra, visualizing it like a lamp being moved.
Extensively performing the Buddha-activities, one should recite the mantra as follows:
while holding both fists covered [at the heart], one should scatter them outward from the chest in two directions, in the manner of the "Exquisite Incense" mudrā. One should then recite this mantra.
Externally, one makes offerings to the various deities; furthermore, one should visualize them in the four corners:
in the southeast is named *Hikhī* (Playful), with both fists at the heart;
in the southwest is *Hasa* (Laughing), with both palms scattered beside the mouth.
The Song-dweller resides in the northwest; holding a *kōṅhōu* lute, he dances in the northeast.
His movements follow the ritual protocol, and his appearance and attire are entirely golden.
Furthermore, the mantra and mudrā are set forth.
Cover both with the two fists and rotate them to the right around the heart;
this is called the Playful Gesture (Līlāmudrā). Its name is as stated hereafter.
As for the previous gesture, place it beside the mouth and slowly release the self-dāna and prajñā fingers.
Lifting the palms and extending the arms to their full length, one recites the mantra with a smile.
Fixing the arms like a *vīṇā* lute, the left hand is slightly bent;
with the right hand in the gesture of plucking the strings, this constitutes the mudrā for singing the *vidyā*.
The two fists dance at the heart; joining them at the crown of the head and then dispersing them is called the mudrā of the dance.
The mantra syllables are then set forth, with four following the command and stationed at the gates.
The ritual forms and deportment shall now be further expounded.
In the east, he holds a hook and is blue in color;
Resplendent and situated in the south, he carries a noose that is entirely yellow; In the west, he grasps a chain which is deep red;
In the north, he is named Kiṅkiṇī (the Bell), possessing a green crown and garland.
The Secret Seal and Mantra: Furthermore, one should now form two fists with the backs pressed together;
hook the thumbs and wisdom-fingers (tarjanīs) in opposition, extend the fingers of strength (madhyamās) fully, and then gradually bend the fingers of progress (anāmikās).
Slightly summoning with this hook-seal (*ākarṣaṇa-mudrā*):
its clarity is as follows—raise the hands as before, cross the fingers of strength (*bala*), and turn them so that the tips hang together like a circular cord; then recite the subsequent mantra.
Improving the force, the fingers hook together; opening the fists with the backs of the hands crossed over the arms, it is then called the "Locking Seal" (*kīla-mudrā*). Recite the mantra as follows:
"The backs [of the hands] touch like a lock. Move them while sounding the *ghaṇṭā* bell, saying: "Oṃ kīlaya vajra hūṃ phaṭ."
Adorned by the Great Sage, with flower-seats, robes,
and other [attendants] as seen before the Honored One; their colors correspond to their physical marks, their forms are distinct,
they possess manifold virtues, and upon their heads they wear the five-Buddha crowns.
When about to construct the maṇḍala, first visualize a full,
radiant moon disc appearing before you. Within it,
contemplate the principal deity seated in half-lotus posture, gazing upon them with a pleasing countenance.
Furthermore, proclaim the seal of samādhi; the mudrās and mantras previously presented before the principal deity should be performed according to the ritual without error.
Next, the seals for the other deities should be established, beginning likewise with the "eye-arrow."
In accordance with that which protects the body, the Great Bliss Seal follows the mind:
bend the thumb (vajra-finger) deeply; first, let the two [fingers] touch back-to-back, and press them together with the wisdom-finger (index finger).
When the seal is correctly formed, accomplishment shall be attained.
With dhyāna pressing upon prajñā, The deep union of the seal constitutes the name.
Kṣitigarbha (Kilimilakṣa) follows, Displaying the marks of Mahāgata;
He advances the hook toward the pāramitā of praṇidhāna, And with strength grasps the tip of kṣānti.
The precept-finger extends to form the needle; Generosity and wisdom join to become straight.
Meditation and insight naturally stand side by side; Each presses upon the fingers of exertion and grace.
The seal is already formed in accordance with the ritual; Do not alter the sequence of the preceding mudrā.
Externally touching the thighs— first the right, then the left likewise—
and internally making offerings with clarity; twisting the sides,
tossing the vajra-palms upward to form the flower mudrā, and scattering downward to become the incense offering.
With meditative concentration and wisdom joined as a lamp, apply scented ointment and, relying upon the chest, perform playful circumambulation and prostration.
With a smile that accords with the vicinity of the mouth, the self-given generosity and wisdom gradually unfold; then, bind the mudrā of song.
Adjusting the strength, slightly bend [the limbs]; advancing with an empty strike between, settle on *khaṭvāṅga*.
With wisdom, perform three *vastra* (garments/flags) aligned with the heart, then whirl in dance.
Having completed the eight offerings, it is finished.
Next, bind the vajra-bond; by slightly bending the forefingers and slowly beckoning, this is the hook seal (*āṅkuśa-mudrā*).
From the bond, the noose (*pāśa*) should arise between the wisdom-finger (*prajñā-aṅguli*) and the power-finger (*bala-aṅguli*); once the seal is formed, it becomes the chain (*śṛṅkhalā*).
Circumambulating with the wisdom and effort fingers, having pinched them together, they are then hooked; again,
forming the firm binding, the wisdom and precept fingers are lowered to the chest and then shaken—
this constitutes the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of the bell.
The Samaya-mantra is the same as the previous Karma-phrase,
in the station of Vajrasattva; both the practitioner’s dwelling place and its surroundings are filled with sixteen deities, standing in a majestic and orderly array.
Furthermore, by merely reciting this supreme and true praise as it is set forth below,
one will swiftly bring all siddhis to completion;
having finished the sound of the recitation, one should contemplate one's own tutelary deity.
With body and mind undistracted, holding the rosary at the heart and performing the empowerment,
one recites the mantra; next, one recites the mantra of one's chosen deity,
holding the beads while abiding in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*).
Do not move the tip of the tongue excessively; let the lips and teeth meet together.
In vajra-speech, free from sound, clearly contemplate the marks and signs.
Do not allow an interval for even a single moment throughout the four periods of the day; let a hundred thousand [recitations] be the limit.
Or even exceeding this; having thus completed the allotted limit for the recitation of the mantra, hold the *mālā* and make a great vow,
then bind the root mudrā and recite the root vidyā seven times.
Furthermore, perform the eight offerings; with a melodious voice, recite praises and present the *argha* water.
Then, for the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) and the various mudrās, form the *samaya-muṣṭi* and, with a single recitation, draw it apart.
Next, bind the *karmamudrā*. Recite three times while opening the hands;
from each [opening], the respective *mudrā* arises. Each one should be released in its own turn.
Next, bind the *visarjanamudrā*: with both hands, form the *vajrabandha*.
With the thumbs and ring fingers held upright like needles, having recited [the mantra], one should toss them upward;
next, one should form the Jewel Mudrā: with both hands in the Vajra-bond, the index and middle fingers are shaped like a jewel, and the thumbs and little fingers are likewise.
The mudrā arises from the heart; place it at the site of consecration.
The hands are joined like a stringing of garlands; this also forms the armor-mudrā for empowerment.
Once the armor has been donned, join the palms and strike three times.
To cause the assembly of noble ones to rejoice,
one attains joy by releasing bonds through this mantra and mudrā. Then, reciting the mantra,
once the noble ones have been respectfully sent forth and the self-consecration is complete:
Then, emerging from the site of enlightenment, one may wander at will and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures;
regulating one's own breath, one should constantly contemplate the Original Honored One in every thought.
O Benevolent One, you should follow and uphold this.
One fascicle of the *Vajraśekhara-prathama-yoga Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-japa-vidhi*.
